title: Herpesvirus Timelines: EBV Antibody Panels and CMV Avidity
summary: Use the heterophile test and EBV-specific antibodies (VCA IgM, VCA IgG, EBNA-1 IgG) to diagnose and date EBV infection, know why EBV PCR is not used for routine mono, and use CMV IgG avidity to date infection in pregnancy.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 64 Hit 2 (EBV staging), Hit 3 (Monospot), Hit 16 (CMV IgM and low-avidity IgG) and Traps 1–2. Checked against Baron 2013 (IDSA/ASM), Panda 2026, Zhou 2026 and Hui 2026. The reviewer says the Monospot is “not recommended in children < 12 years”; Baron 2013 says false negatives are most frequent in younger children and recommends EBV-specific serology — the lesson teaches that. Not taught: EBNA-1 appearing 6–12 weeks after infection (not in the sources read) and Trap 4 (VCA IgG-only), because Zhou 2026 classifies VCA IgG-positive, IgM-negative results as past infection.

objectives: Interpret a heterophile (Monospot) result and choose follow-up when it is negative in a young child.
Date EBV infection from VCA IgM, VCA IgG, EA IgG and EBNA-1 IgG patterns.
Explain why EBV DNA PCR is not used to diagnose routine infectious mononucleosis.
Use CMV IgG avidity to distinguish recent primary from past infection in pregnancy.

scenes.title: Mono, or not mono?
scenes.altText: Two patient cards. Left: a 17-year-old with fever, sore throat, swollen neck nodes and atypical lymphocytes; Monospot ordered. Right: a 4-year-old with the same picture; Monospot negative. A third card: a pregnant woman with a positive CMV IgM on routine testing. Question token: “Which antibody, which timeline?” The cartoon scientist holds three serum tubes.

cues.text: A teenager has fever, sore throat, swollen neck glands and atypical lymphocytes. A four-year-old has the same picture, but the Monospot is negative.
And a pregnant woman has a positive CMV IgM on a routine test. Is it a new infection that could harm the baby?
Herpesviruses stay for life, so the question is never just yes or no. It is when. Antibody timelines answer that.

scenes.title: The heterophile test: fast, but not for everyone
scenes.altText: A Monospot card: the Monospot detects heterophile antibodies that appear in EBV mononucleosis. A positive result may be considered diagnostic. A caution card: up to 10% are falsely negative — most often in younger children. Two follow-up arrows: EBV-specific serology on the same sample, or repeat the Monospot 7–10 days later. A crossed-out token: “EBV DNA PCR to diagnose routine mono” — viral DNA can be found in healthy carriers, so PCR is kept for immunocompromised patients and atypical cases.

cues.text: The Monospot is a rapid test for heterophile antibodies, which appear during EBV mononucleosis.
A positive Monospot in a typical case may be considered diagnostic of EBV infection.
But up to one in ten is falsely negative, most often in young children. That is our four-year-old.
Next step: EBV-specific antibodies on the same sample, or repeat the Monospot a week or so later.
Do not use EBV DNA PCR to diagnose routine mono. Healthy people who were infected long ago can carry viral DNA. PCR is for immunocompromised patients and atypical cases.

props.label: ✗ EBV DNA PCR for routine mono

scenes.title: Reading the EBV panel like a clock
scenes.altText: A timeline from infection onward, with three antibody tokens rising at different times: VCA IgM (early, then fades), VCA IgG (early, lifelong), EBNA-1 IgG (late, lifelong). Pattern cards: Primary (current/recent) — VCA IgM positive (and/or EA IgG), EBNA-1 IgG negative. Past — VCA IgG and/or EBNA-1 IgG positive, VCA IgM and EA negative. Reactivation — EBNA-1 IgG positive with EA IgG and/or VCA IgM. A caution token: VCA IgM alone cross-reacts (e.g., CMV, dengue) — use the full panel.

cues.text: EBV antibodies arrive in a set order. IgM against the viral capsid antigen, VCA, comes early and then fades.
VCA IgG also comes early but stays for life. Antibody to the nuclear antigen, EBNA-1, comes late and also stays for life.
So VCA IgM with no EBNA-1 means a current or recent primary infection. EBNA-1 has not had time to appear.
VCA IgG or EBNA-1 IgG without VCA IgM means an old infection. EBNA-1 together with IgM or early-antigen antibody suggests reactivation.
Never trust VCA IgM alone. In one study, a third of positive results were false, from cross-reaction with CMV or dengue. Read the whole panel.

props.title: Reactivation
lines: EBNA-1 + with EA or VCA IgM

scenes.title: CMV in pregnancy: IgM is not enough — measure avidity
scenes.altText: A CMV card: about 5% of pregnant women have a detectable CMV IgM, and most do not have a recent primary infection. An avidity card: IgG avidity measures how tightly IgG binds — a marker of recency, not protection. Low avidity → infection typically within the past 3 months; high avidity → more than 3 months earlier (maturation varies). Primary infection = seroconversion (IgG newly positive) or IgM + IgG with low avidity. A caution: a high-avidity result in the 2nd or 3rd trimester cannot exclude a primary infection in early pregnancy — test stored early-pregnancy serum if available. Patient: IgM +, IgG +, avidity high → past infection > 3 months before (first-trimester sample).

cues.text: Now the pregnant patient. About 5 percent of pregnant women have a detectable CMV IgM, and most of them do not have a new infection.
So a positive IgM is followed by an IgG avidity test. Avidity measures how tightly the IgG binds. It is a clock, not a measure of protection.
Low avidity means the infection was probably within the past three months. High avidity means it was earlier, though maturation varies between people.
A primary infection is shown by seroconversion, or by IgM plus IgG with low avidity. That carries the highest risk for the baby.
Our first-trimester sample shows IgM, IgG and high avidity: a past infection. But a high avidity late in pregnancy cannot rule out an early primary infection.

props.title: CMV IgM + in pregnancy
lines: ≈ 5% of pregnant women · most not recent

props.title: Primary infection
lines: Seroconversion, or IgM + IgG with low avidity

props.label: 1st trimester: IgM + · IgG + · high avidity → past infection

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards appear in turn: “EBV DNA PCR to diagnose mono” (✓ serology; DNA is found in healthy carriers); “A negative Monospot in a 4-year-old rules out EBV” (✓ false negatives are common in young children — use EBV-specific serology); “CMV IgM positive in pregnancy = primary infection” (✓ check IgG avidity; most IgM positives are not recent).

cues.text: Trap one: order EBV DNA PCR to diagnose mono. No. Use serology; healthy people can carry EBV DNA.
Trap two: a negative Monospot rules out EBV in a four-year-old. No. False negatives are most common in young children; order EBV-specific antibodies.
Trap three: a positive CMV IgM in pregnancy means primary infection. No. Most are not recent; check IgG avidity.

props.title: ✗ “EBV DNA PCR to diagnose mono.”
lines: ✓ Serology · DNA found in healthy carriers

props.title: ✗ “Negative Monospot in a 4-year-old rules out EBV.”

scenes.title: Capsid comes first, nucleus comes last
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Capsid comes first, nucleus comes last.” VCA antibodies appear early; EBNA-1 appears late — so EBNA-1 present means the infection is not new. And for CMV: “Avidity ages the antibody.” A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: capsid comes first, nucleus comes last. VCA antibodies appear early; EBNA-1 appears late, so EBNA-1 means the infection is not new. And for CMV: avidity ages the antibody.
Where it breaks: some people never make EBNA-1 or lose it, especially when immunocompromised; IgM can cross-react or persist; avidity maturation varies; and kits differ in cut-offs.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: EBNA-1 may be absent or lost (immunocompromised)
IgM cross-reacts or persists · avidity maturation varies

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Monospot + = EBV mono · negative in young kids → EBV serology · no PCR for routine mono”, “VCA IgM + EBNA-1 − = primary · EBNA-1 + = old · CMV IgM → avidity (low = ≤ 3 months)”.

cues.text: Diagnose mono with the Monospot or EBV-specific serology, date EBV infection by VCA IgM versus EBNA-1, and date CMV infection in pregnancy with IgG avidity rather than IgM alone.

props.label: Monospot + = EBV mono · negative in young kids → EBV serology · no PCR for routine mono
VCA IgM + EBNA-1 − = primary · EBNA-1 + = old · CMV IgM → avidity (low ≤ 3 mo)

explanation.what: Plain language: herpesviruses stay in the body for life, so tests ask when the infection happened. Scientific terms: heterophile antibodies (Monospot rapid test), viral capsid antigen (VCA) IgM and IgG, early antigen (EA) IgG, Epstein–Barr nuclear antigen 1 (EBNA-1) IgG, cross-reactivity, CMV IgG avidity, seroconversion.
explanation.why: Antibody responses mature in sequence: IgM first, IgG later, and antibodies to some antigens (EBNA-1) only after weeks. IgG binding strength (avidity) increases over months. Latent EBV DNA persists in healthy carriers, so DNA detection does not prove acute disease.
explanation.measure: Monospot: positive may be considered diagnostic; up to 10% false negatives (young children) → EBV-specific serology or repeat in 7–10 days. EBV patterns: primary = VCA IgM and/or EA IgG positive, EBNA-1 negative; past = VCA IgG and/or EBNA-1 positive, VCA IgM and EA negative; reactivation = EBNA-1 positive with EA and/or VCA IgM. CMV: low IgG avidity ≈ infection within ~3 months; high avidity > 3 months.
explanation.differs: Primary vs past vs reactivated EBV; true vs cross-reactive VCA IgM; recent vs remote CMV infection.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: VCA IgM+/EBNA-1− = acute; EBNA-1+ = not acute; negative Monospot in a toddler; PCR not for routine IM; CMV IgM+ with low avidity in pregnancy.

comparisons.title: CMV IgG avidity

right.label: High avidity
points: Late in pregnancy cannot exclude early primary

comparisons.distinguisher: How tightly IgG binds, as a recency clock.

mnemonic.text: Capsid comes first, nucleus comes last — and avidity ages the antibody.
mnemonic.explanation: VCA antibodies appear early, EBNA-1 late; CMV IgG binds more tightly as it ages.
mnemonic.limitation: EBNA-1 may be absent or lost; IgM cross-reacts or persists; avidity maturation varies; kit cut-offs differ.

takeaway: Diagnose mono with the Monospot or EBV-specific serology, date EBV infection by VCA IgM versus EBNA-1, and date CMV infection in pregnancy with IgG avidity rather than IgM alone.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old with pharyngitis and lymphadenopathy has VCA IgM positive, VCA IgG positive and EBNA-1 IgG negative. What is the interpretation?

options.text: Current or recent primary EBV infection
options.rationale: Correct. VCA IgM without EBNA-1 IgG indicates primary infection; EBNA-1 appears late.
Incorrect. Past infection is VCA IgM negative, usually with EBNA-1 IgG.
Incorrect. Reactivation patterns include EBNA-1 IgG.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old with fever, pharyngitis and atypical lymphocytes has a negative Monospot. What is the best next step?

options.text: EBV-specific serology (VCA IgM, VCA IgG, EBNA-1 IgG)
options.rationale: Correct. Heterophile false negatives are most common in young children.
Incorrect. A negative Monospot does not exclude EBV in a young child.

options.text: Plasma EBV DNA PCR to diagnose mono
options.rationale: Incorrect. EBV DNA can be found in healthy carriers; serology is preferred in immunocompetent patients.

options.text: Repeat the Monospot the same day
options.rationale: Incorrect. A repeat is useful only after 7–10 days.

questions.stem: In the first trimester, a woman has CMV IgM positive, CMV IgG positive and low IgG avidity. What does this indicate?

options.text: Probable primary CMV infection within about the past 3 months
options.rationale: Correct. IgM and IgG with low avidity indicate recent primary infection.

options.text: Past infection more than 3 months ago
options.rationale: Incorrect. That pattern has high avidity.

options.text: A false-positive IgM with no infection
options.rationale: Incorrect. Low-avidity IgG supports a genuine recent infection.
Incorrect. Low avidity points to a recent infection, not long-standing immunity.

references.usedFor: Serologic classification: uninfected (EBNA-1, VCA IgG, EA IgG negative); primary (EA IgG and/or VCA IgM positive, EBNA-1 negative); past (EA IgG and VCA IgM negative, VCA IgG and/or EBNA-1 positive); reactivation (EBNA-1 positive with EA IgG and/or VCA IgM).

references.usedFor: ≈ 5% of pregnant women have detectable CMV IgM, most without recent primary infection after avidity testing; avidity measures binding strength as a marker of recency, not antibody efficacy; primary infection = seroconversion or IgG + IgM with low avidity; low avidity ≈ within 3 months, high > 3 months, maturation varies; high avidity in 2nd/3rd trimester cannot exclude early primary infection — test booking serum.

claims.text: Positive Monospot may be considered diagnostic; up to 10% false negatives, mostly in young children; follow with EBV serology or repeat in 7–10 days.
EBV DNA can be found in healthy seropositive people; serology is primary in immunocompetent patients; PCR for immunocompromised or atypical cases.
EBV patterns: primary, past, reactivation; VCA IgM alone cross-reacts (CMV, dengue).
CMV IgM in ≈ 5% of pregnancies, mostly not recent; avidity as recency clock; low ≈ ≤ 3 months; primary = seroconversion or IgM + low-avidity IgG; late high avidity cannot exclude early primary.
EBNA-1 IgG appears 6–12 weeks after infection; heterophile antibodies agglutinate sheep/horse red cells; Monospot not recommended under 12 years.
claims.note: Not taught; the lesson says only “young children” for the Monospot limit. Details not in the sources read.
